RT @EuromaidanPress: Ukraine needs more fighter jets now, Zelenskyy told its allies on 17 November: 40 more F-16s, and more Mirages. The jets exist, but their owners aren't letting go.

Ukraine flies about 31 F-16s, and around half are in repair on any given day. Another 66 are pledged, but the last of Belgium's 53 may not arrive until 2029.

Greece has more than 40 Mirage 2000s it has retired or expects to retire. Athens has shrugged at every request from Kyiv.

France still flies around two dozen. A few more of those are the best Ukraine can hope for soon, David Axe writes.

Sweden's first Gripens are due early next year. The Rafales, not before 2028.

tweets.content:
New lecture on pwncollege, presented by guest lecturer Jennifer Miller (Zolutal) from the SEPCOM lab, provides an introduction to Linux kernel security and exploitation concepts within the context of the CSE466 course (0:00-0:15).

Key takeaways from the lecture:

> Kernel Basics: The kernel acts as the interface between hardware and userland applications, handling task scheduling and interprocess communication (1:08-1:36).

> Kernel Modules: These are extensions to the kernel, ranging from drivers to security modules. They can be in-tree (part of the kernel source) or out-of-tree (proprietary/external) (2:46-3:51).
Interacting with Modules: The lecture demonstrates how modules expose functionality to user space, specifically through `/proc` entries and the `ioctl` system call (3:51-6:07).

Exploitation Concepts:
> Privilege Escalation: A primary goal, often involving the manipulation of the `task_struct` and `cred` structures to set the effective UID to 0 (root) (11:03-13:09).

> Memory Protections: Discusses mitigations like KASLR (Kernel Address Space Layout Randomization), which randomizes memory positions (15:08-16:00).

> Kernel Shellcoding: Unlike user space, kernel shellcode calls internal kernel functions directly. The lecture demonstrates allocating RWX (Read-Write-Execute) memory pages and triggering execution through a modified kernel module (8:51-11:03, 42:00-58:50).

> Debugging: The lecture provides practical guidance on using GDB to interact with the guest kernel, noting the challenges of debugging with hardware-assisted virtualization and the benefits of using emulator mode (7:55-8:41, 51:42-55:17).

https://t.co/1YLN8pCvce

tweets.content:
RT @MasonRaziel: ارتش آمریکا با چند تریلیون دلار بودجه جرأت نکرد یه گوشی رو ۴۸ ساعت به شبکه‌ی چین وصل کنه؛ اون‌ وقت ما در ایران با فیلترشکن رایگان خیال می‌کنیم ناشناسیم. پروتکل واقعی سفر شنژن را ببینید:

طبق پروتکل‌های ضدجاسوسی واشنگتن، خاک چین منطقه‌ای آلوده از نظر سایبری به حساب می‌آید و هیچ مقام آمریکایی اجازه ندارد گوشی شخصی، لپ‌تاپ یا حتی کابل شارژش را از هواپیما بیرون ببرد. به همه‌ی اعضای هیئت گوشی یک‌بارمصرف می‌دهند و موقع برگشت، همه‌ی دستگاه‌ها و کارت‌های تردد را پیش از ورود به کابین جمع می‌کنند و از بین می‌برند. این حساسیت در پایان نشست ۱۹ نوامبر شنژن به جایی رسید که حتی گوشی خبرنگاران همراه ترامپ هم پای پله‌های هواپیما ضبط شد تا هیچ وسیله‌ای که به دکل یا وای‌فای چین وصل شده، به آمریکا برنگردد (گزارش هیئت رسانه‌ای کاخ سفید در پایان سفر شنژن).

اما ماجرا فقط به گوشی‌ها محدود نمی‌شود؛ ترامپ هیچ غذا یا نوشیدنی‌ای را که میزبان آماده کرده باشد، نمی‌خورد و نمی‌نوشد. نگرانی سرویس مخفی فقط سم نیست؛ ردیاب‌های نانویی و برداشتن نمونه‌ی دی‌ان‌ای از لیوان و ظرف‌ها برای ساختن پرونده‌ی ژنتیکی و پزشکی او هم مطرح است. گفت‌وگوهای حساس را در اتاقک‌های سیارِ ضدشنود انجام می‌دهند و بعد از فرود در آمریکا، همه‌ی اعضای هیئت دوباره بررسی‌های کامل ضدجاسوسی را می‌گذرانند تا هیچ اثری از نفوذ ۴۸ ساعته باقی نماند (پروتکل‌های حفاظتی و ضدجاسوسی سفرهای پرخطر آمریکا).

نقطه‌ی کور ماجرا همین‌جاست: همان فناوریِ تفتیش عمیق اینترنت، شنود مخابراتی و آلوده‌کردن سخت‌افزار که واشنگتن را وادار می‌کند گوشی‌هایش را فیزیکی نابود کند، همان زیرساختی است که پکن سال‌هاست به تهران می‌فروشد و حالا پشت سیم‌کارت‌ها، اپ‌های داخلی و فیلترشکن‌های رایگان قرار دارد.

وقتی سرویس مخفی آمریکا به وای‌فای و حتی لیوان آب پکن اعتماد ندارد، یعنی در یک شبکه‌ی آلوده هیچ سپر نرم‌افزاری ارزانی وجود ندارد. فرقِ در امان ماندن و آسیب‌دیدن فقط به این بستگی دارد که این واقعیت را قبل از دیر شدن بفهمی یا بعدش.

اما ماجرا فقط به گوشی‌ها محدود نمی‌شود؛ ترامپ هیچ غذا یا نوشیدنی‌ای را که میزبان آماده کرده باشد، نمی‌خورد و نمی‌نوشد. نگرانی سرویس مخفی فقط سم نیست؛ ردیاب‌های نانویی و برداشتن نمونه‌ی دی‌ان‌ای از لیوان و ظرف‌ها برای ساختن پرونده‌ی ژنتیکی و پزشکی او هم مطرح است. گفت‌وگوهای حساس را در اتاقک‌های سیارِ ضدشنود انجام می‌دهند و بعد از فرود در آمریکا، همه‌ی اعضای هیئت دوباره بررسی‌های کامل ضدجاسوسی را می‌گذرانند تا هیچ اثری از نفوذ ۴۸ ساعته باقی نماند (پروتکل‌های حفاظتی و ضدجاسوسی سفرهای پرخطر آمریکا).

نقطه‌ی کور ماجرا همین‌جاست: همان فناوریِ تفتیش عمیق اینترنت، شنود مخابراتی و آلوده‌کردن سخت‌افزار که واشنگتن را وادار می‌کند گوشی‌هایش را فیزیکی نابود کند، همان زیرساختی است که پکن سال‌هاست به تهران می‌فروشد و حالا پشت سیم‌کارت‌ها، اپ‌های داخلی و فیلترشکن‌های رایگان قرار دارد.

وقتی سرویس مخفی آمریکا به وای‌فای و حتی لیوان آب پکن اعتماد ندارد، یعنی در یک شبکه‌ی آلوده هیچ سپر نرم‌افزاری ارزانی وجود ندارد. فرقِ در امان ماندن و آسیب‌دیدن فقط به این بستگی دارد که این واقعیت را قبل از دیر شدن بفهمی یا بعدش.

RT @Huntio: 🚨 China-Linked Armory Castle Exploits VMware vCenter Zero-Day for Admin Access

https://t.co/4us2jzLEpG

The China-linked threat actor Armory Castle (formerly UNC5221) exploited CVE-2026-123890, a critical VMware vCenter authentication bypass (CVSS 9.8).

Using a custom Golang tool called BONESAW, attackers gained administrator access, extracted the vCenter LMDB database, and hijacked SAML authentication.

The campaign also involved lateral movement through compromised Linux appliances, custom backdoors, and data theft from ESXi systems.

The activity dates back to September, but Broadcom only released patches on November 19, over two months later.

#ThreatIntel #VMWare #ZeroDay #CyberSecurity

Hence why using something like weightless/GLP where you can switch back on the stock model, it's much more efficient. 

If obliteration is not done properly, you will start to damage the capabilities of the model. 

Very simple to understand. Super clear. Great job. Thank you.

quotedTweet.rawContent:
CNN has now published its second extraordinary NSA story in a single week. This time, a former NSA hacker claims that AI agents bypassed 2FA. Let me explain why this is disinformation put out by the US government, using simple logic.

David Kennedy claims AI agents found a vulnerability that allowed them to bypass 2FA.

App based 2FA can only be bypassed through reverse proxy phishing, which I first wrote about on behalf of the PKI Consortium in 2019. People who believe apps such as Google Authenticator and 1Password protect them from phishing are mistaken. FIDO hardware security keys are phishing-resistant.

But Kennedy isn’t claiming phishing was involved. He’s claiming that AI agents discovered a vulnerability that allowed them to “bypass 2FA”.

Unless Kennedy identifies the specific 2FA service that was breached, or the security company itself publicly discloses the vulnerability, we should assume this story is disinformation. 

Even AI with another 20 years of research and quantum capabilities wouldn’t be able to bypass 2FA. That would take a vulnerability in the authentication service. But that’s not what we’re being told.

Here’s how app based 2FA works. When you activate it, the authentication service and your authenticator app share a secret key. The app uses that key and the current time to generate a 6 digit code, usually every 30 seconds. 

The server independently calculates the expected code and checks it against the one you enter. There are 1 million possible combinations, but the server limits failed attempts and rejects codes outside the accepted time window. AI can’t calculate the correct code without the secret key. It can’t bypass the server’s verification by guessing faster either.

Even AI with another 10 years of research and quantum computing capabilities couldn’t bypass 2FA. That would take a serious vulnerability in the service’s authentication implementation, not the underlying TOTP algorithm.

What vulnerability is he talking about? Which authentication product did they bypass?

If Kennedy discovered a serious vulnerability, he has a professional responsibility to notify the affected company so it can fix the problem. That company also has a duty to publicly disclose the vulnerability.

Kennedy also claims the AI agents stole company data and encrypted an entire file system in 14 minutes. This is noise. Focus on his claims about bypassing 2FA.

He hasn’t provided the technical evidence for anything.

3 days earlier, CNN reported that 6 sources had disclosed problems with the NSA’s highly classified internal communications network.

I find it astonishing that people believe 6 sources independently disclosed problems with one of the US’s most sensitive intelligence networks to CNN. If classified information about those networks was disclosed as reported, the people responsible would face serious prison sentences. And the NSA doesn’t seem bothered by such a disclosure. Does this mean Snowden can come home? 

Now CNN is promoting another extraordinary cybersecurity story through someone who previously worked for the NSA, this time bombastic claims about AI agents that supposedly defeated a security system that’s impossible to bypass.

2 NSA related stories on CNN in one week, both with serious national security implications and neither supported by any public technical evidence for independent verification.

If the claims about AI agents turn out to be false, that makes the timing of CNN’s earlier NSA story even more suspicious.

Who benefits from frightening the public into believing that conventional cybersecurity protections are no longer effective against AI?

🚨 We are observing probing of Apache Roller for CVE-2026-129448, the unauthenticated RCE that Apache has warned is exploited in attacks.

The requests POST a serialized Java object to /roller-services/xmlrpc using the ex:serializable extension type. The object is an empty placeholder class, so this is a check for whether the server deserializes untrusted data before auth. That pathway is the exploit surface for the RCE.

If you run Roller, upgrade to 6.1.6. If you can't, remove the XML-RPC servlet mapping. Disabling XML-RPC in the admin UI does not block this.

tweets.content:
I think there’s a major misunderstanding in this discussion.

The growing number of vulnerabilities discovered in open source software doesn’t necessarily mean that open source code is worse than proprietary software.

What we’re seeing is a massive increase in scrutiny.

For years, many open source projects simply didn’t receive thorough security reviews. Nobody had the time, resources or financial incentive to look that closely.

Now anyone with access to a capable LLM can point it at a public repository and start looking for vulnerabilities. And newer models are getting remarkably good at finding issues that previous tools and human reviewers missed.

But something very similar is happening behind closed doors.

I can tell you from our own experience, and from discussions with people at other software companies, that internal development teams are also struggling with a flood of findings from AI-assisted code reviews.

Many of these findings concern code that has been running in production for years. In proprietary software development, they rarely become public CVEs or security advisories. They end up as Jira tickets, creating backlogs that take weeks or months to process.

Ironically, while AI accelerates software development, it’s also slowing teams down by exposing years of accumulated technical debt and security issues that nobody had identified before.

So I’d be careful about interpreting the current wave of open source vulnerabilities as evidence of lower code quality.

quotedTweet.rawContent:
They contained the host. I still had the network.

My CODE BLUE 2026 talk "Pass-the-Device" is now public: slides (EN/JA), 5 recon tools, experimental Sigma + KQL detections.
https://t.co/i9GOCnUofD

The idea: device trust is not device binding.

From one compromised, enrolled laptop there are two routes off the host:
A) copy existing state: cert, cookie, client config
B) enroll a new client with the user's SSO
Both end on a machine with no EDR. Each leaves a different record to revoke.

The goal is practical: to know where the trust boundaries are, to know the limits of what your VPN/SASE solution can do, and to understand which configuration you need.

Two real cases, Cisco and Zscaler: host isolated, account disabled, and the second session stayed alive. A fresh VPN/SASE enrollment is persistence outside EDR.

Three checks for defenders this week:
1. Do your VPN/SASE, enrollment and IdP logs reach the SIEM at all?
2. Compare every device enrolled in the last 90 days with your managed-device inventory.
3. Add one line to the IR playbook: end the user's VPN/SASE sessions and revoke the enrollments, not only the host.

Thank you @codeblue_jp.

#codeblue_jp #codeblue2026

tweets.content:
RT @danlovesproofs: We spent two days trying to hack ourselves with abliterated models. The biggest risks we found, by far, were side channels into our infra, outside the application code.

Stuff like:
- The oneoff dev env we set up to test out Coder that had way too much access
- CI runners had tailnet access for no good reason

We’ve scanned our application code many times over, but there were a lot of scary risks hiding in these side doors and third party vectors. All problems that were very easy to mitigate once we were aware of them.

Many of the high-profile hacks from the past two weeks happened this way. Application code held up fine, but the company had a massive breach due to a vulnerability in a vibecoded internal tool or an unpinned CI dependency or third party js or …

You’ll see us incorporating this pov into our vuln scans. (And of course we’ll continue perpetually trying to hack ourselves!)

tweets.content:
when you are operating on a red team, think of the potential consequence of every single action. not taking action is generally good. there are ops when time is a factor, but in most cases, i think its good to simply pause, wait, think. 

you should think about the possible consequence of any action, no matter how 'small'. every action after successful initial infection, is likely logged, somewhere. every single thing you do, is inevitably 'seen' at some level. the difference in your success is whether or not it is bubbled up to a human or automated security product with response capability.

now of course, you can get a sense of some small actions that are consistently 'safe'. but i would caution against trusting your mental list so quickly. it is easy to become complacent, to think 'this is always safe' without really considering all the variables or unknowns, of your current environment. take pause. reassess. 

the idea should be to take the time and spend the mental effort, to imagine the possible downsides, visibility, artifacts, any possible IOCs that will be generated. build a confidence level for that next considered action. reassess if you have other options to achieve the same effect. in fact, do you even need this piece of data or escalation? perhaps not? is there a safer way to reach the same goal? these are the questions to ask yourself before you make the next move.

quotedTweet.rawContent:
Jeff Bezos on why too many ideas can destroy a company, and the "releasing the work" framework that saved Amazon:

"Jeff Wilke came to me one day and said, 'You have enough ideas per minute, per day, per week to destroy Amazon.'"

"I was like, 'What do you mean?' He's like, 'You have to release the work at the right rate that the organization can accept it.'"

"His view of the world was every time I released an idea, I was creating a backlog, a queue, work in process. And because it was just stacking up, it was adding no value, and in fact it was creating distraction."

"And so I started prioritizing the ideas better, keeping lists of them, keeping them to myself until the organization was ready for the ideas. And then I also started figuring out, how can I build an organization that can be ready for more ideas?"

"But that idea of 'releasing the work' was very profound for me, and it made us operationally more effective while still being inventive."

Shannon McCormick from Anduril brought a fascinating forensic investigation to @objective_see ! 🔍

When AI agents can execute commands, read files, and access the network, checking which process ran is only half the investigation.

The real detective work? Connecting the prompts to what the agent actually did. 🕵️

And my favorite takeaway:

Your AI assistant might need an alibi before it needs another prompt. 😂

Great research, Shannon! 🌴🔥

#macOS #AISecurity #DFIR #OBTS

RT @Mu55sy: 🕵️‍♀️ The antivirus said CLEAN. @PwnieFan said HOLD MY COFFEE. ☕😂

Another brilliant session wrapped up at @objective_see ! 🌴🍎

Megan showed why malware detection isn’t a popularity contest where 70 antivirus engines get to vote.

🔍 Suspicious behavior tells a story.
🌐 Network traffic leaves clues.
🧠 OSINT connects the dots.

And sometimes, the malware nobody flagged is the one worth investigating most.

The biggest threat isn’t always what your tools detect. It’s what you stop questioning. 🎯

Maui’s got beautiful beaches, but Megan brought the real treasure hunt! 🏝️

#macOS #ThreatHunting #AppleSecurity  #OBTS

tweets.content:
MIT researchers found a CPU side-channel called Interrupt Injection that cuts straight through Spectre v2 defenses on both AMD and Intel chips.

By arranging a hardware interrupt to arrive precisely at the right moment, unprivileged user-space code can re-poison the branch predictor after the defense has executed but before the CPU relies on the prediction. 

The timing window exists in the gap between OS implementation and CPU protection. You can pull Linux password hashes from kernel memory despite modern mitigations.
